news_drafts.headline: Wiltshire expects £90.5m special needs grant on 30 November, with about £10m still to find by March 2028
news_drafts.lead:
Wiltshire Council expects a £90.5m government grant on 30 November 2026 related to its deficit on special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) spending, its mid-year treasury report to Cabinet says. The grant is subject to audit. The paper says it will repay short-term loans from other councils maturing in November and December, and elsewhere gives £75m of temporary loans as the main use. The budget monitoring report puts the grant at £90.326m and says the £3.942m left over "will be set aside to offset deficits accrued before the end of the statutory override period (31st March 2028)". The override is a government rule that keeps a schools-funding deficit off a council's main balance sheet.

The deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, stood at £86.384m at the end of 2025/26, after government Safety Valve payments and the council's agreed contribution. The surplus arises because that contribution was higher than the 10% the new grant conditions require. For 2026/27 the council forecasts a £5.785m overspend in high needs, the part of school funding for SEND, up £1.410m from quarter one. A £5.698m early years underspend reduces the overall deficit, which is forecast at £1.458m above the plan submitted to the Department for Education. Placement and support costs will be validated before quarter three.

The treasury paper says the deficit is having an "ever-increasing impact on the cash held by the council". It puts the council's under-borrowed position at £219.245m at 30 September 2026 and says that cannot be maintained indefinitely. The council's chief finance officer estimates it "will need to find approximately £10m" by 31 March 2028, assuming government support for 90% of the deficit. Arrangements for deficits accrued in 2026/27 and 2027/28 are not yet confirmed.

news_drafts.headline: Wiltshire Council holds £10m LOBO loan at 4.45% with a lender option date in December 2026
news_drafts.lead:
Wiltshire Council has a £10m loan whose lender, the bank PBB Deutsche Pfandbriefbank, can propose a new interest rate in December 2026. The council's mid-year treasury management report to the Finance and Procurement Select Committee says: "There is a reasonable risk that the lender will exercise their option in December."

The loan is a LOBO, a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The loan currently carries a 4.45% coupon, the interest rate fixed in the loan terms, and runs to 10 December 2052, according to the report's Appendix 1.

The report says that if the rate rises above the rates of the Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils, the council will repay the principal. It does not say the option has been exercised or what rate has been proposed. It does not give the cost of any replacement funding.

news_drafts.headline: Wiltshire says its high needs reserve will not cover the schools-funding deficit projected for March 2028
news_drafts.lead:
Wiltshire Council's high needs reserve will not be enough to meet the schools-funding deficit projected for March 2028, according to the strategic risk summary put to its Audit and Governance Committee on 6 October. The council says overspending on support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) is exceeding the high needs allocation, the part of its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) set aside for that support.

The council has submitted a SEND Reform Plan to the Department for Education. Under it, 90% of the deficit as at 31 March 2026 would be written off, and the remaining 10% met from the council's high needs reserve, money it has put aside for that purpose. The paper states: "The council's earmarked reserve is not sufficient to meet the projected deficit at the end of the statutory override." The statutory override is a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, and it ends in March 2028. The papers say no government guidance has yet explained how deficits built up between March 2026 and March 2028 will be handled.

The council has also changed how it describes the risk. Its strategic risk on demand for education, health and care plans, the legal documents setting out a child's support needs, has been renamed, redefined and rescored. In the council's words, it "now focuses more broadly on provision of support for children with SEND within available budgets."

findings.headline: The £0.793m pay award pressure (additional 0.3%) is included in the quarter two forecast and carries an ongoing impact on base budgets.
findings.detail: The paper says pay budgets are under considerable stress, compounded by the vacancy factor target. The ongoing cost must be built into base budgets as part of the 2027/28 MTFS.
findings.matters: A pay award above budget adds to every council's base budget going forward, so the size of the gap an additional 0.3% creates is directly comparable across councils.
findings.figures: £0.793m pay award pressure; additional 0.3% pay award
findings.quote: As reported last quarter, the £0.793m pressure associated with the pay award (additional 0.3%) is included within the forecast.

findings.headline: Car parking forecasts a £0.961m underspend, a favourable movement of £0.732m from quarter one, with approved tariff increases included.
findings.detail: The paper says car parking usage has stayed in high demand since the tariff increases, continuing a trend from 2025/26 driven by new machines, new payment options and additional enforcement officers. Parking bay suspensions for utility works are also generating income.
findings.matters: It is a clear case of a fees and charges income line beating budget, which other councils budgeting for similar tariff changes can compare against.
findings.figures: £0.961m underspend; £0.732m favourable movement from quarter one
findings.quote: Car Parking services are currently forecasting an underspend of £0.961m

findings.headline: £1.500m drawdown from the Treasury Reserve to offset the shortfall in Crisis Resilience Fund funding after the final settlement came in lower than budgeted
findings.detail: Cabinet is asked to approve this drawdown. The Crisis Resilience Fund replaced the Household Support Fund from April 2026, and the paper seeks to move its budget from Finance, Revenues and Benefits to Leisure, Culture & Communities.
findings.matters: A government grant settlement coming in below budget and being covered from a treasury reserve is a funding shortfall other councils running similar grant-funded schemes may face.
findings.quote: A drawdown of £1.500m from the Treasury Reserve to offset the shortfall in Crisis Resilience Fund funding

findings.headline: The Transformation Reserve is forecast to fall to approximately £0.6m after the council funds over £2.4m of transformation activity from it in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The S151 officer notes that MTFS commitments extend beyond the remaining reserve balance and will need detailed review as future budget proposals are developed. The reserve was partly used to fund the 2024/25 year-end overspend and must be repaid as opportunities arise.
findings.matters: A reserve funding transformation that falls to a small balance while commitments continue constrains how far the council can rely on transformation to close future gaps.
findings.figures: over £2.4m drawn for transformation activity; approximately £0.6m remaining balance
findings.quote: The impact of the drawdown in 2026/27 will result in a balance on the reserve of approximately £0.6m.

findings.headline: A £2.220m saving has been identified following restructuring of loans, against a £0.720m net interest overspend.
findings.detail: The net interest overspend reflects a higher interest rate environment than assumed at budget setting. A £1.000m drawdown from the Treasury volatility reserve is proposed to support it. Finance & Investment Income & Expense is forecast at £8.418m against an £11.888m budget.
findings.matters: A loan restructuring that yields a saving at this scale is a specific borrowing action a finance director at another council may want to understand, and it shows how the council is managing interest costs.
findings.figures: £2.220m restructuring saving; £0.720m net interest overspend; £1.000m reserve drawdown; £11.888m budget; £8.418m forecast
findings.quote: A £2.220m saving has been identified following restructuring of loans
